Diagnose a column of CPR numbers

Source: R/diagnose_cpr.R
diagnose_cpr.Rd

Reports what is wrong with a vector of CPR numbers before it is used as a join key or passed on: how many are missing, which are malformed and why, and the signs that a column has been through Excel or a numeric conversion on the way. It is the question to ask of a CPR column you did not produce yourself.

Usage

diagnose_cpr(x, as_of = Sys.Date())

Arguments

x

A vector of CPR numbers, typically a column such as df$pnr. Numeric vectors and factors are converted with as.character() first.

as_of

The date the data describes, as a Date or an ISO date string (YYYY-MM-DD). Birth dates after it, or more than 120 years before it, are flagged. Defaults to today.

Value

A pnr_diagnosis object, printed as a short report. It is a list with n (the number of values), checks (a data frame with one row per check: check, kind ("problem" or "note"), n, and rows, a list column of row numbers), distinct (the number of distinct valid numbers), birth_range (the earliest and latest valid birth date), male_share (the share of valid numbers with an odd final digit), and as_of.

Details

Every value gets exactly one status. These problems sum to the length of x:

  • valid: ten digits encoding a real birth date, after the same cleaning as clean_cpr(). Validity is the same as in add_cpr_info().

  • missing: NA, or empty once dashes and spaces are removed.

  • scientific: written in scientific notation, such as "1.11111E+09". Excel and some exports do this to long numbers. The trailing digits are gone and cannot be restored; the source has to be read again with the column as text. "1111111118.0" and similar decimal forms are counted here too.

  • wrong_length: only digits, but not nine or ten of them.

  • non_digit: contains characters other than digits, dashes and spaces.

  • invalid_date: ten digits, but the first six are not a real date.

The notes overlap with the problems and with each other. They are not errors, but each says something about where the data has been:

  • zero_restored: nine digits, padded with a leading zero. Birth days 01-09 make about a third of all CPR numbers start with a zero, and Excel drops it from numeric cells.

  • separators: contained dashes or spaces.

  • mod11_fails: valid, but fails the modulus-11 check. Since 2007 the CPR office issues numbers that do not satisfy it, so this is not an error by itself (https://cpr.dk). A large share among older birth dates can still point to typing errors.

  • repeated: valid values that occur more than once. Expected in a panel with one row per person and year, a problem in a table of persons.

  • born_after_as_of and older_than_120: valid numbers whose decoded birth date is implausible for the data. These are usually typing errors that happen to form a real date, or a wrong as_of.

The diagnosis never prints a CPR number, only counts and row numbers, so its output can go into a log. The row numbers of every check are kept in the returned object.

See also

clean_cpr(), add_cpr_info()

Examples

x <- c("0101004007", "010100-4007", "101004007", "1.01004E+08",
       "3102004007", "12345", "ukendt", NA, "1111111118")
diagnose_cpr(x, as_of = "2025-01-01")
#> ── CPR diagnosis ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ! 4 of 9 valid (2 distinct)
#> ✖ 1 missing (row 8)
#> ✖ 1 in scientific or decimal notation: digits are lost, read the source again as text (row 4)
#> ✖ 1 with the wrong number of digits (row 6)
#> ✖ 1 with characters other than digits, dashes and spaces (row 7)
#> ✖ 1 with ten digits but no real birth date (row 5)
#> ℹ 1 had lost a leading zero (Excel), restored by cleaning (row 3)
#> ℹ 1 contained dashes or spaces (row 2)
#> ℹ 3 valid, sharing their CPR number with another row (rows 1, 2, 3)
#> Birth dates 1911-11-11 to 2000-01-01; 75.0% male.

# The rows behind a check
d <- diagnose_cpr(x, as_of = "2025-01-01")
d$checks$rows[d$checks$check == "scientific"][[1]]
#> [1] 4
